title: The Rise of Nationalism in Europe — Chapter Summary
intro: In 1848 Frédéric Sorrieu sketched peoples of Europe paying homage to Liberty. His vision — a world of free, self-governing nations — captures 19th-century Europe's great political idea: NATIONALISM. This chapter traces that idea from the French Revolution and Napoleon's reforms, through the liberal-nationalist revolutions of 1830 and 1848, to the unification of Italy and Germany, and finally to the explosive Balkans where nationalism became a narrow, imperialist creed that helped trigger the First World War.

branches.label: Revolutions 1830 + 1848
details: Defeated, but demand for nation-state remained

sections.heading: The French Revolution and the Idea of the Nation
bullets: 1789 — sovereignty shifted from the king to the PEOPLE.
Ideas of la patrie (the fatherland) and le citoyen (the citizen).
New tricolour flag replaced the royal standard.
Centralised administration with uniform laws and a common system of weights and measures.
French (as spoken in Paris) made the common national language.

sections.heading: Napoleon and the Civil Code
bullets: 1804 — Civil Code (Napoleonic Code) abolished privileges of birth, secured equality before the law and the right to property.
In occupied lands, feudalism was abolished, peasants freed from serfdom and manorial dues.
Uniform weights, measures and currency aided trade and the new business class.
But conscription, censorship, taxation and loss of political freedoms turned enthusiasm into hostility.

sections.heading: The Making of Nationalism — Middle Class and Romanticism
bullets: Mid-18th-century Europe — kingdoms, duchies and cantons; multi-ethnic Habsburg Empire.
A new EDUCATED MIDDLE CLASS championed liberty, equality and constitutional government.
ROMANTICISM celebrated emotion, folk culture, language as the soul of the nation (Herder, das Volk).
In partitioned Poland, the Polish language became a weapon of national resistance.

sections.heading: The Age of Revolutions — 1830 and 1848
bullets: Population growth, unemployment and slum-cities created economic hardship.
1830 — JULY REVOLUTION in France; BELGIUM broke away from the Netherlands.
GREECE won independence (Treaty of Constantinople, 1832); supported by Lord Byron and other West Europeans.
1848 — uprisings in Paris, Vienna, Berlin, Italian states.
FRANKFURT parliament drafted a constitution for Germany; rejected by Prussia's king and dispersed.
Women organised, demonstrated and published — but were denied SUFFRAGE.

sections.heading: Unification of Germany and Italy
bullets: Nationalism in the late 19th century was harnessed by CONSERVATIVES for state-building.
GERMANY — Bismarck of Prussia, three wars (1864 Denmark, 1866 Austria, 1870–71 France).
January 1871 — Wilhelm I proclaimed German Emperor at Versailles.
ITALY — Mazzini's Young Italy failed; Cavour and Victor Emmanuel II of Sardinia-Piedmont, with French alliance, defeated Austria (1859).
Garibaldi's volunteers won the south (1860); Italy unified in 1861 under Victor Emmanuel II.

sections.heading: Britain — A Different Story
bullets: Britain's nation-state was forged through a long, slow process.
Act of Union 1707 — England and Scotland → United Kingdom of Great Britain.
1801 — Ireland forcibly incorporated.
Symbols (Union Jack, God Save Our Noble King, English language) promoted a 'British nation', with English culture dominant.
Older identities — Welsh, Scot, Irish — survived as subordinate partners.

sections.heading: Visualising the Nation and Imperial Nationalism
bullets: Artists personified nations as female allegories — MARIANNE for France, GERMANIA for Germany.
Marianne = red cap, tricolour, cockade; on coins and stamps, in public squares.
Germania = crown of oak leaves (heroism).
Late 19th century — nationalism became a narrow, intolerant creed used to further IMPERIALIST aims.
Balkans — Slav nationalisms + Ottoman decline + great-power rivalry → First World War (1914).

key_takeaways: The French Revolution made the people the source of sovereignty and gave Europe the modern idea of a nation.
Napoleon's Civil Code (1804) carried the principles of equality, property and uniform law across Europe.
Nationalism was driven by an educated middle class (liberty + constitution) and by Romantic culture (folk + language).
The 1830 and 1848 revolutions were largely defeated, but made the demand for nation-states impossible to ignore.
Italy (1861) and Germany (1871) were unified by conservative state-building — Cavour/Garibaldi and Bismarck.
Britain's nation-state grew slowly through the Acts of Union (1707, 1801) under English dominance.
Nations were given a face through female allegories — Marianne for France, Germania for Germany.
By the late 19th century, nationalism became narrow and imperialist; Balkan rivalries triggered WWI in 1914.

glossary.definition: The political idea that a people sharing language, culture or history should form a single self-governing nation-state.
A state in which the majority of its citizens — and not only its rulers — come to share a common identity and history.
A form of monarchical rule, usually centralised, militarised and repressive, in which the king's power is unlimited.
A direct vote by which all the people of a region are asked to accept or reject a proposal.
An abstract idea (such as Liberty or a Nation) given concrete form, often as a person — for example, Marianne for France.
The female allegory of France, marked by the red cap of liberty, the tricolour and the cockade.
The female allegory of Germany, wearing a crown of oak leaves to symbolise heroism.
Relating to a common racial, cultural or linguistic identity within a population.
Napoleon's 1804 code abolishing privileges of birth, establishing equality before the law and the right to property.
An early-19th-century cultural movement that emphasised emotion, intuition and folk culture over Enlightenment rationalism.
A political belief that traditional institutions — monarchy, church, family, property — must be preserved.
A 19th-century political belief in liberty, equality before the law, constitutional government and individual rights.
The political process by which several states were brought together to form one nation-state — as in Italy 1861 and Germany 1871.
The right to vote in elections.
The region of south-east Europe, mostly under the Ottoman Empire, that became a flashpoint of competing nationalisms before 1914.
